# Diagnosing Intermittent Window Motors in a Subaru Forester XT

When the driver's window on a Right-Hand Drive (RHD) Subaru Forester XT refuses to move immediately upon engaging the switch, or exhibits a distinct latency before activating, it is almost never a software glitch. Automotive glass lifters operate on purely electromechanical principles; there is no embedded logic to execute, and no code to debug. However, understanding the signal path from the interior switch to the motor assembly allows you to isolate whether the issue lies in power delivery, mechanical resistance, or sensor contamination.

The symptom of a delayed responseâwhere the window sits still for a couple of seconds before suddenly dropping into gearâis a classic signature of voltage drop under load. When you press the switch, the control module sends a signal, but if the motor is fighting friction or the connection has high resistance, the system might momentarily reset or fail to latch until the voltage stabilizes. This behavior distinguishes itself from a completely dead circuit, which would result in no movement at all.

A frequent culprit in these scenarios, even when the battery test confirms the vehicle starts reliably, is poor grounding. The window motor requires a dedicated ground path to complete its circuit. If the chassis ground strap near the door jamb has corroded or if the terminal on the lift regulator itself is loose, the resistance spikes during operation. This is analogous to a developer encountering a race condition where timing is off; the system works sporadically when conditions align perfectly but fails when load increases.

The source material notes that the rear windows exhibit a different pattern: they simply do not work or function perfectly without hesitation. The owner correctly identifies this as "dirty switches." This distinction is vital for diagnosis. Front window motors often integrate with the power window master switch, which can develop internal carbon tracking issues or loose contacts over time. When you press the front driver's switch and feel a faint click but see no movement, check the wiring harness at the door hinge first. The constant flexing of the rubber boot causes wires to fatigue and eventually break internally, creating an intermittent open circuit that mimics software lag.

To troubleshoot this without replacing the entire assembly immediately, inspect the lift regulator mechanism. If the window glass is binding due to dried lubricant or a bent guide, the motor will struggle against mechanical resistance, leading to the observed delay. A simple application of silicone spray to the sash guides can restore smooth movement and eliminate the voltage drop caused by excessive load.

Furthermore, verify the condition of the switch contacts. If the rear windows are failing due to dirt, the front driver's switch may be suffering from similar oxidation. Cleaning these contacts with electrical contact cleaner often resolves the "nothing happens for a couple of seconds" symptom without needing new parts. Always unplug the connector before cleaning to avoid shorting pins.

If the battery is confirmed healthy and the grounds are secure, the motor itself might be drawing excessive current as its brushes wear down. In that case, swapping the regulator assembly is the most reliable fix. While aftermarket switches can be installed, ensure they match the original pinout and resistance specifications of the Forester XT to avoid triggering the vehicle's overload protection.

Finally, consider the possibility of a failing Body Control Module (BCM) if multiple windows begin behaving erratically simultaneously. However, given that the rear windows only fail completely or work perfectly, the issue is isolated to the front driver's circuit. Prioritize checking the physical connections and mechanical alignment before assuming electronic failure.
